units.text: INT. SUPERMAN - CONTINUOUS
You won't get it, my boy, if Ramsden upsets the will.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: Ha! I see. You have got me in a cleft stick.
units.name: RAMSDEN

units.text: He leaves me nothing but the charge of Ann's morals, on the ground that I have already more money than is good for me. That shows that he had his wits about him, doesn't it?
units.name: TANNER

units.text: grimly.
I admit that.
units.name: RAMSDEN

units.text: rising and coming from his refuge by the wall.
Mr Ramsden: I think you are prejudiced against Jack. He is a man of honor, and incapable of abusing--
units.name: OCTAVIUS

units.text: Don't, Tavy: you'll make me ill. I am not a man of honor: I am a man struck down by a dead hand. Tavy: you must marry her after all and take her off my hands. And I had set my heart on saving you from her!
units.name: TANNER

units.text: Oh, Jack, you talk of saving me from my highest happiness.
units.name: OCTAVIUS

units.text: Yes, a lifetime of happiness. If it were only the first half hour's happiness, Tavy, I would buy it for you with my last penny. But a lifetime of happiness! No man alive could bear it: it would be hell on earth.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: violently.
Stuff, sir. Talk sense; or else go and waste someone else's time: I have something better to do than listen to your fooleries
units.name: RAMSDEN

units.text: he positively kicks his way to his table and resumes his seat.
You hear him, Tavy! Not an idea in his head later than eighteen-sixty. We can't leave Ann with no other guardian to turn to.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: I am proud of your contempt for my character and opinions, sir. Your own are set forth in that book, I believe.
units.name: RAMSDEN

units.text: eagerly going to the table.
What! You've got my book! What do you think of it?
units.name: TANNER

units.text: Do you suppose I would read such a book, sir?
units.name: RAMSDEN

units.text: Then why did you buy it?
units.name: TANNER

units.text: I did not buy it, sir. It has been sent me by some foolish lady who seems to admire your views. I was about to dispose of it when Octavius interrupted me. I shall do so now, with your permission.
units.name: RAMSDEN

units.text: He throws the book into the waste paper basket with such vehemence that Tanner recoils under the impression that it is being thrown at his head.
You have no more manners than I have myself. However, that saves ceremony between us.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: He sits down again.
What do you intend to do about this will?
units.name: TANNER

units.text: May I make a suggestion?
units.name: OCTAVIUS

units.text: Certainly, Octavius.
units.name: RAMSDEN

units.text: Aren't we forgetting that Ann herself may have some wishes in this matter?
units.name: OCTAVIUS

units.text: I quite intend that Annie's wishes shall be consulted in every reasonable way. But she is only a woman, and a young and inexperienced woman at that.
units.name: RAMSDEN

units.text: Ramsden: I begin to pity you.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: hotly.
I don't want to know how you feel towards me, Mr Tanner.
units.name: RAMSDEN

units.text: Ann will do just exactly what she likes. And what's more, she'll force us to advise her to do it; and she'll put the blame on us if it turns out badly. So, as Tavy is longing to see her--
units.name: TANNER

units.text: shyly.
I am not, Jack.
units.name: OCTAVIUS

units.text: You lie, Tavy: you are. So let's have her down from the drawing-room and ask her what she intends us to do. Off with you, Tavy, and fetch her.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: Tavy turns to go.
And don't be long for the strained relations between myself and Ramsden will make the interval rather painful
units.name: TANNER

units.text: Ramsden compresses his lips, but says nothing--.
Never mind him, Mr Ramsden. He's not serious.
units.name: OCTAVIUS

units.text: He goes out.
RAMSDEN [very deliberately] Mr Tanner: you are the most impudent person I have ever met.
seriously.

I know it, Ramsden. Yet even I cannot wholly conquer shame. We live in an atmosphere of shame. We are ashamed of everything that is real about us; ashamed of ourselves, of our relatives, of our incomes, of our accents, of our opinions, of our experience, just as we are ashamed of our naked skins. Good Lord, my dear Ramsden, we are ashamed to walk, ashamed to ride in an omnibus, ashamed to hire a hansom instead of keeping a carriage, ashamed of keeping one horse instead of two and a groom-gardener instead of a coachman and footman. The more things a man is ashamed of, the more respectable he is. Why, you're ashamed to buy my book, ashamed to read it: the only thing you're not ashamed of is to judge me for it without having read it; and even that only means that you're ashamed to have heterodox opinions. Look at the effect I produce because my fairy godmother withheld from me this gift of shame. I have every possible virtue that a man can have except--
units.name: TANNER

units.text: I am glad you think so well of yourself.
units.name: RAMSDEN

units.text: All you mean by that is that you think I ought to be ashamed of talking about my virtues. You don't mean that I haven't got them: you know perfectly well that I am as sober and honest a citizen as yourself, as truthful personally, and much more truthful politically and morally.
units.name: TANNER
